items.title: Harry "Sweets" Edison interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995
items.q: Like Coleman Hawkins. Like Bunny Berigan. Like Benny Goodman... They all had a sound that they could be recognized.

ctx.x: How do you feel about that? How did that effect the music? Do you think it was a —

Oh, it had its toll on jazz because there are no more big bands, there are I think only the Count Basie Band and the Duke Ellington Band, but it’s not like the leader was there, like if you cut the head of a snake off, the tail dies, and the head of the snake was like the band leader, like Count Basie. Regardless what he played when he was there, you miss © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

seeing him. He had an aura about him that everybody loved. Everybody loved Count Basie. Everybody loved Duke Ellington. The big bands were so popular in those days, until, and they, most of the musicians in those days demanded respect because they were an artist. And they were all individualists. Everybody had a sound of their own. They could be identified on the record like if Billie Holiday would sing on the record you’d know it’s nobody but Billie Holiday. items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: Bunny Berigan was good. ... he played -- he was a stylist. ... I think Bunny Berigan made the best record on 'Can't Get Started With You' than anybody.

ctx.x: Well, the one trumpet player, the one white trumpet player that --
Yeah, now there was a guy that sounded like Louie. He was exceptional.
